extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature and practising scientists (naturalists, geneticists, geologists, chemists, astronomers)
extracted.subtask_description: A mixed-genre Nature magazine page containing letters, brief notes and short articles that give practical experimental methods, interpretive criteria, editorial/style recommendations (transliteration), and judgments about useful features of technical books. Useful for guidance on how to perform or evaluate short scientific communications and simple experimental tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a practical technical book on lubricants/oils
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient is given to enable the chemist to carry out these tests in ‘the orthodox manner and to reduce the results. The book should also be of value to the engineer, who must understand the meaning of the experimental results; his requirements are considered in later chapters on the selection of lubricants and oils employed in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful work for users of oils should be brief and clear and present the principal properties; avoid overly comprehensive and highly technical treatments that are of little service to users. Ensure procedures are sufficient for chemists to perform standard tests and for engineers to interpret results; include practical selection guidance for applied use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical method to test Wegener’s fittings and coincidences (modelling-wax/plasticine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to the distortion present in all maps such tests must be carried out on a globe. An easier plan is to roll out a lump of modelling wax or plasticine into a sheet of moderate thickness. The sheet may then be pressed upon the globe and cut to the required shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut the sheet a little smaller than the area to be represented so that the actual margin appears all round it and build it outwards to this margin by adding small pieces of wax. Old plasticine that is rather dry works well and does not stick to the globe. Tracing paper is difficult and often requires cutting and slashing to fit; modelling wax gives an easier, more faithful test of fit/congruence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and construction of triangular compasses for precise spherical measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Much more precise tests can be carried out with the help of some form of triangular compasses. The three points of the compasses may be placed on three critical points of the globe and afterwards transferred, without altering their relative positions, to any other part of the globe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A convenient instrument can be constructed from a one‑jointed two‑foot rule: fix a point about an inch long near the joint; provide each arm with a sliding carrier bearing a short sleeve through which a pointed rod (e.g., a knitting needle) slides rather stiffly. The three rods form the points and should stand approximately at right angles to the plane of the rule. Better forms use arms that are arcs of circles concentric with the globe so the points have fixed lengths and avoid troublesome adjustments. Ordinary draughtsman's triangular compasses are of little use on a spherical surface. Using such compasses increases precision and shows whether high plasticity would be required to produce the proposed coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental criteria for studying opalescence in liquid mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Einstein's thermodynamical treatment gives an expression for light‑scattering due to spontaneous local fluctuations of concentration; but corrections for the fluctuations of density of each component and for molecular anisotropy must be added. Very near the separation temperature concentration fluctuations dominate; at higher and lower temperatures density fluctuations and molecular anisotropy become substantial contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating experiments on opalescence: measure light‑scattering over a wide temperature range (including temperatures well above the critical point), record polarization changes (expect an increase in the proportion of unpolarized light as one moves away from the critical temperature), and test frequency dependence (molecular anisotropy may be a function of incident light frequency). Compare results with Einstein‑Smoluchowski theory plus the stated corrections. Seek confirmation across multiple mixtures (e.g., phenol‑water) and note prior experimental confirmations (V. S. Tamma, Seshagiri Rao, W. H. Martin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for transcription (transliteration) of Russian scientific names in English publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Russian scientific names should not be rendered inconsistently across journals by adopting Czech-type diacritics that many English newspapers and books cannot typeset. What is wanted in this country is an intelligible British system of transcription, uniform for all Russian names alike: and this we have ready-made in the R.G.S. II. system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a system that is practical for British/English publications (readable with common type and understandable to Britons), uniform across journals and newspapers, and consistent for scientific, literary, musical names and place‑names. Avoid adopting foreign orthographies (e.g., Czech diacritics) that are not widely available in English founts or that cause inconsistent rendering; consider R.G.S. II as the recommended practical standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive criteria for dark nebulae and obscuration by interstellar dust
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark markings and starless regions are produced by interposition of huge obscuring clouds (dust). Of various forms of distributed matter, fine dust is by far the most efficient in producing obscuration because it has the greatest superficial area per unit mass. For clouds of the same mean density the opacity reaches a sharp maximum when the particles are of a particular size; for visual light the maximum opacity occurs when the radius is 0-086 (text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting obscuration: consider dust particle radius and density, the factor q that accounts for size‑to‑wavelength complications (g≈1 when particles are more than two or three wavelengths in diameter; qg/γ is maximal when circumference equals the wavelength), and the transition from non‑selective to selective absorption (selective varying as λ^-4). Quantitatively, a cloud of particles of the optimum size and density of rock can produce one magnitude of absorption with only 1/86 milligram per cm^2 cross‑section. Also account for radiation pressure (for optimum‑sized particles of water density, solar radiation pressure may be ~10× gravitational attraction) and spectral‑type dependence (radiation pressure differs by stellar class). Use distance estimates (parsecs) and consider reddening of embedded stars when dense luminous nebulosity is present.
